background.definition: Actinic or solar keratoses (AKs) are rough, scaly patches appearing on sun-exposed skin. Appearing skin-color to red to brown, AKs represent focal areas of abnormal keratinocyte proliferation. AKs are considered a premalignant condition with low risk of progression to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC).

list.listitem: Incidence: 60% in Australians over age 40
Incidence: 149/1000 persons/year in the UK
Number of lesions increases directly with age in men, but not women.
Prevalence studies in the UK found prevalences of 19% to 24% in Galway, South Wales, and Merseyside.
Most common premalignant skin condition
Cumulative sun exposure
UVB-specific mutations found in AK lesions
Epidermal cells demonstrate disordered arrangement and maturation.
Changes are restricted to epidermis, and range only from basal layer to full-thickness.
Neoplastic cells penetrating into dermis define SCC but do not penetrate beyond the dermis.
Daily use of sunscreen (SPF-16 or -17) reduces the number of AKs over a period of 7 months to 2 years. A
Daily use of sunscreen (SPF-15 or higher) decreases the incidence of cSCC over a period of 4.5 years. B
Suspect AK in patients with rough, scaly patches of skin in sun-exposed areas. C
Consider performing a skin biopsy in cases of clinical uncertainty, when invasive cutaneous malignancy is suspected, or for treatment-refractory lesions. C

Differential.Differential_Features: More well circumscribed, thicker, and more firm lesion than AK; may bleed more easily or be painful and may be ulcerated
More erythematous and with a fine raised border that may appear pearly; may be ulcerated
More likely to be asymmetric and ulcerated

list.listitem: Diagnosis is primarily made clinically.
Rough, scaly patches of skin present, usually 1 to 2.5 cm in diameter but may become confluent.
AK patches are usually normal skin tone but may range to reddish brown.
AKs are often asymptomatic but may become mildly painful or pruritic.
AKs may often be more easily felt than seen.
Dermoscopy features of AK have been described but not compared with biopsy results.

Skin biopsy is recommended for atypical lesions (eg, ulcerated, bleeding), lesions that are persistent or progressive despite adequate treatment, or if there are concerns about overt cutaneous malignancy.
Diagnosis is based on clinical appearance (rough, scaly patches of sun-exposed skin) and a gritty, sandpaper-like sensation on palpation.
Skin biopsy is recommended for atypical lesions, or if there is a concern regarding overt malignancy, or progression to malignancy.

Treatment is not mandatory, given the low rate of malignant transformation, although most physicians and patients opt for treatment when AKs are diagnosed. A Cochrane review found no evidence that treatment reduces the likelihood of invasive cSCC. B
Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is likely more effective and has better cosmetic outcome than cryotherapy for individual AKs. B

Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen, nitrous oxide, or carbon dioxide) is useful for solitary or few scattered AKs. The cure rate is 69% for treatment of more than 5 seconds and 83% for freeze times over 20 seconds. Longer freeze times lead to more post-treatment hypopigmentation. B
Data from a network meta-analysis and a head-to-head trial of field-directed therapies for AKs affecting the scalp and face suggest that 5% 5-FU cream is the most effective treatment. A
Topical therapy is useful for large areas or numbers of lesions.

5-fluorouracil (5-FU) appears to be the most effective treatment for multiple AKs. This network meta-analysis conclusion was based on the outcome of participant complete clearance which is a good patient-oriented outcome.
A RCT (non-blinded) found clinical clearance rates of 68% for cryosurgery, 85% for imiquimod, and 96% for 5-FU.

Additionally, a head-to-head trial of field-directed therapies for AKs involving the head demonstrated the highest efficacy (defined as >75% reduction in AKs after 12 months) for 5% topical 5-FU (74.7%), followed by 5% imiquimod (53.9%), methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy [MAL-PDT] (37.7%), and 0.015% ingenol mebutate (28.9%).
5% 5-FU is applied twice daily for 2 to 4 weeks. The common reaction is local irritation, with dryness, erythema, pain, or skin erosions appearing cosmetically undesirable during treatment.

Other formulations of 5-FU are available (1%, 0.5%), but studies of efficacy are limited. One study used pretreatment topical 0.5% 5-FU for 1 week before cryosurgery and found it reduced the number of actinic keratoses still present at 6 months.
Ingenol mebutate is a plant sap extract, and is effective for patients with multiple, closely spaced actinic keratoses (NNT = 2 compared with placebo).

A prospective randomized controlled study, treating 25 cm2 contiguous field in 100 patients, compared ingenol mebutate gel OD for 3 days and 5-FU twice daily for 4 weeks with similar rates of tolerability and safety for pruritus and pain with eyelid oedema higher in the ingenol mebutate group. Local skin reactions peaked day 4 and resolved by day 15 for ingenol mebutate gel and peaked day 29 and lasted till day 36 for 5-FU.

A single study of diclofenac (an NSAID) 3% topical gel applied twice daily for 90 days showed up to 50% patients with total resolution of lesions. The treatment was well tolerated with milder symptoms of pruritus, skin dryness, and rash than with 5-FU.

A few studies (all manufacturer sponsored) of imiquimod 5% cream applied twice or three times a week for 16 weeks showed 45% to 57% complete resolution and 64% to 72% partial resolution of AK lesions. Side effects are similar to 5-FU, but the cost is higher. A comparison of cryotherapy with imiquimod in 71 patients found better cosmetic outcomes with imiquimod but a better 12 month clearance rate with cryotherapy (85% vs. 67%, p <0.01).

A systematic review evaluating field-directed therapy for actinic keratosis found 1 RCT (N=702) demonstrating the efficacy of topical tirbanibulin 1% daily for 5 days in producing 100% clearance after 2 months in 54% of treatment patients compared to 9% for placebo (NNT = 2). However, recurrence of treated lesions was 47% and new lesions within the treatment area was 42% after 1 year. Adverse events were similar between groups and were minor (i.e., local skin reactions) and resolved by the end of the trial. A 5-day course of topical tirbanibulin is around $1,020 (goodrx.com, 5/25/26).
HPV vaccination, based on a small RCT (N=70), may decrease AKs in immunocompetent patients with multiple lesions.

Similarly, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), based on a small prospective cohort study (N=23), may decrease the number of AKs in immunocompetent adults starting ICIs for any active cancer. The authors acknowledge that more studies are necessary to establish the use of ICIs as an immunopreventive strategy for individuals at risk for skin cancer, especially considering its toxicity and cost.

Photodynamic therapy is effective in up to 91% of AKs in trials comparing it with cryotherapy. Photodynamic therapy is likely to be more expensive than most other therapies, but it may be useful when AKs are numerous or located at sites of poor healing such as the lower leg. It may also provide better cosmetic outcomes than cryotherapy.

Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen, nitrous oxide, or carbon dioxide) is useful for solitary or few scattered AKs. The cure rate is 69% for treatment of more than 5 seconds and 83% for freeze times over 20 seconds. Longer freeze times lead to more post-treatment hypopigmentation.

A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 13 RCTs involving 1,380 patients compaed interventions for nonscalp, nonface AKs. The authors concluded that cryotherapy has the highest participant complete clearance rate (RR 7.7; 95% CI 3.2-18; 10 studies; I2 = 20.3%).

Topical intervention (eg, 5-FU, diclofenac, ingenol mebutate) applied after cryotherapy appears to increase the complete clearance of AKs from 46% to 79% (NNT = 3), based on low-quality evidence from a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs.
Curettage and/or electrodesiccation may be useful for single, possibly thicker lesions. The risks are similar to those of cryotherapy.
Observation is an option. Regression is 100 times more likely than progression to SCC. Early thin, solitary, or few lesions are candidates for observation for spontaneous resolution.

The British Academy of Dermatology guidelines do not identify a single best treatment. Options for field treatment of larger areas include chemical peels, and topical and systemic retinoids; options for lesion treatment include antimitotic in collodion, cryosurgery, curettage, and excision; while topical therapies and photodyamic therapy may be used in either situation. Cost and patient preference are important consideration.
Low cost interventions include observation, emollient creams, 5% 5-FU, and the combination of 5-FU and salicylic acid 10%. Higher cost options for treatment include PDT and imiquimod.

Application of photosensitizing cream (preferentially absorbed by neoplastic cells), followed by exposure to appropriate wavelength of light, causes cell death. Approved agents include aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and methyl aminolevulinate (MAL). Frequently the treatment is painful. The outcomes are similar to cryotherapy, but the cost is considerably higher. A Cochrane did find that PDT provided superior cosmetic outcomes to cryotherapy for the treatment of individual AKs. PDT may be useful for large areas of confluent AKs.
A small RCT with 37 patients did a within patient comparison of PDT with placebo, and found that it was effective for AKs on the dorsal hands.

A randomized trial compared 35% trichloroacetic acid peel (TCA) with ALA-PDT for 28 patients with multiple AKs. After 12 months, a blinded assessment of cosmetic outcomes found significantly greater reduction in total lesion count (58% vs. 31%, p = 0.006) and a greater likelihood of complete clearance (74% vs. 49%, p = 0.011) with ALA-PDT.
Around 0.1% to 0.5% of AKs show malignant transformation to a squamous cell carcinoma over a year, while 25% to 70% of AKs show spontaneous regression over 1 to 4 years. B
However, 15% to 50% of AKs that regress reappear over the next year. B
The patient with 8 AKs has a 10% probability of at least one transforming to SCC over 10 years. There is no way to distinguish which AKs are more likely to progress to SCC. B
